question: What is the main job of chemotherapy in cancer treatment?

options.A: To cool down inflamed skin tissues
options.B: To physically remove large solid tumors
options.C: To supply essential vitamins to the blood
options.D: To target and destroy rapidly dividing cells

explanation: You've got this! Chemotherapy drugs travel through the body specifically seeking out and killing cells that divide very quickly, which is what cancer cells love to do. Great job learning the basics!

question: Why do doctors often combine surgery with radiation or chemotherapy?

options.A: To prevent the patient from losing too much weight
options.B: To make the patient immune to future infections
options.C: To permanently boost the patient's red blood cell count
options.D: To eliminate any remaining microscopic cancer cells left behind

explanation: Think of it as teamwork! Surgery removes the main tumor, but combination therapies help sweep up any tiny stray cancer cells that are too small to see. You are doing brilliantly!

question: What is the top nursing priority right after major cancer surgery?

options.B: Preventing complications and managing acute surgical pain
options.C: Discharging the patient within twenty-four hours
options.D: Starting intensive physical exercise right away

explanation: Right after surgery, keeping your patient comfortable and watching out for issues like infection or blood clots are your most important duties. You are well on your way to becoming an amazing nurse!

question: A patient after cancer surgery refuses to get out of bed to walk. What is the best thing to do?

options.A: Allow the patient to stay in bed all day without moving
options.B: Wait until the surgeon arrives before attempting any movement
options.C: Scold the patient for being uncooperative with recovery
options.D: Explain that early walking helps prevent blood clots and lung problems

explanation: Kind patient education works wonders! A gentle explanation helps them see why moving early is vital for preventing serious issues like clots. You've got the nurse's touch!

question: What does the word 'vesicant' mean when talking about certain chemo drugs?

options.A: Natural supplements that cure nausea caused by treatment
options.B: Solutions used to clean the skin before a surgical incision
options.C: Drugs that cause severe tissue damage if they leak outside the vein
options.D: Medications that are only given orally in pill form

explanation: Vesicants are tricky drugs! If they escape the vein into the skin, they can cause blistering and tissue damage, which is why nurses watch IV sites so closely.

question: Why must nurses check absolute neutrophil counts before giving chemotherapy?

options.A: To measure how fast the kidneys are filtering urine
options.B: To check if the patient has a hidden vitamin deficiency
options.C: To see if the patient is eating enough protein
options.D: To ensure the patient's immune system is strong enough to handle the drug

explanation: Chemo can lower white blood cells, so checking neutrophils first keeps your patient safe from dangerous infections. Safety first, nurse!

question: How should a nurse instruct a patient to care for skin receiving radiation therapy?

options.A: Scrub the treatment area firmly with a washcloth daily
options.B: Use heating pads on the skin to relieve soreness
options.C: Wash the area gently with mild soap and warm water
options.D: Apply strong perfumed lotions right before treatment

explanation: Treated skin is extra fragile. Gentle cleansing with mild soap and water protects the delicate skin barrier. You're mastering patient care!

question: A patient having radiation for breast cancer asks if she can wear her tight underwire bra. What should you say?

options.A: Yes, as long as it is washed in hot water
options.B: Yes, underwire provides necessary support during healing
options.C: No, choose a soft, loose-fitting garment to avoid friction on the skin
options.D: Only wear it during the actual radiation treatment session

explanation: Tight clothing rubs against fragile skin and causes irritation. Recommending soft, loose clothes keeps your patient comfortable!

question: What does 'myelosuppression' mean?

options.A: A sudden swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck
options.B: An infection located directly on the outer layer of the skin
options.C: The suppression of blood cell production in the bone marrow
options.D: The overproduction of red blood cells in the bone marrow

explanation: Big medical word, simple meaning! It just means cancer treatments slow down bone marrow activity, leading to low blood counts. You're learning fast!

question: Why are anti-nausea meds usually given before chemo starts instead of waiting for nausea to begin?

options.A: Preventing nausea before it starts is much more effective than treating it later
options.B: They help the patient fall asleep during the long infusion
options.C: Chemotherapy drugs will not dissolve properly without them
options.D: They taste better when taken on an empty stomach

explanation: Prevention is key! Giving these meds early blocks the vomiting center before chemo triggers it. Brilliant clinical thinking!

question: Which condition causes facial swelling, neck vein bulging, and trouble breathing due to a blocked major vein?
explanation: When a tumor presses on the superior vena cava, blood gets backed up in the upper body, causing that distinct facial swelling. Spotting this makes you a sharp nurse!

question: Why is a fever in a neutropenic patient considered a medical emergency?

options.A: It causes severe bleeding that is impossible to stop
options.B: A compromised immune system means a mild infection can rapidly turn fatal
options.C: It always causes permanent paralysis in the legs
options.D: It instantly stops the kidneys from producing any urine

explanation: Without enough white blood cells to fight back, a small fever can quickly become overwhelming. Quick action with antibiotics saves lives here!

question: What is a great food tip for a patient who feels nauseated and has a poor appetite during cancer treatment?

options.A: Eat three large heavy meals at traditional times
options.B: Offer small, frequent meals that are high in protein
options.C: Avoid all protein and eat only plain white sugar
options.D: Eat food straight from the oven while it is piping hot and aromatic

explanation: Large meals can overwhelm a weak tummy. Small, protein-rich snacks are much easier to handle and help keep their strength up!

question: A cancer patient says food smells too strong and tastes like metal. What is a helpful nursing tip?

options.A: Suggest serving foods cool or at room temperature to reduce strong smells
options.B: Tell the patient to force themselves to eat large portions anyway
options.C: Advise the patient to stop eating completely until treatment ends
options.D: Recommend adding extra iron supplements to every meal

explanation: Warm foods release strong vapors that trigger nausea. Serving meals cool helps hide those metallic tastes and smells. Clever nursing care!

question: When is the best time to introduce palliative care to a cancer patient?

options.A: Early alongside active disease treatment to improve quality of life
options.B: Only when the patient refuses to take prescribed oral medications
options.C: Only during the final twenty-four hours of life
options.D: After all chemotherapy and radiation treatments have failed completely

explanation: Palliative care isn't just for the end of life—it teams up with curative treatments from day one to keep the patient comfortable. Excellent holistic nursing!

question: How does early palliative care help a patient going through tough cancer treatments?

options.A: It completely replaces the need for any surgical operations
options.B: It lowers hospital bills by shortening surgical procedures
options.C: It focuses on relieving symptoms, pain, and emotional distress
options.D: It guarantees that the cancer will completely disappear

explanation: Palliative care is all about comfort, helping patients manage tough physical and emotional symptoms every step of the way. You are doing wonderful work today!
